title: The Lazy Engineer
body_markdown:
#### PART 5 of 5


*Why the best engineers refuse to do the work*


In the middle of a college lecture, almost as an aside, one of my professors stated that the best engineers are extremely lazy. Give a lazy engineer a hard, repetitive job, and they won’t do it. They’ll build something that does it for them. Build a system. Don’t do the work.


I’ve been trying to live up to it ever since, and my definition of lazy has grown along the way. The first time it really paid off, all I wanted was to stop writing a report. It ended up changing my career.


### A week every quarter


At the refinery, every engineer owned a set of KPIs for their units and defended them in a review every quarter. The heads of engineering, operations, and planning spent an hour or more drilling into every trend. It felt like a cross-examination of my judgment as much as of the units’ performance.


Getting ready ate the entire week beforehand. We updated the graphs, noted each trend, put them in the report, and wrote the same standard text every report had. The only part that mattered, explaining what drove each trend, came last.


I got sick of it, so I wrote an Excel macro. It updated my graphs and dropped them into the report with the standard text. It even wrote a footnote under each graph saying whether the KPI had gone up, gone down, or held steady. Wherever my explanation belonged, it left an XXX in bright red so I couldn’t miss one. Every XXX marked the one thing the macro couldn’t write — the why.


### Two hours’ notice


One day, the economics and planning group from Delta, which owned our refinery, came on site. Someone had the bright idea that they should sit in on a quarterly KPI review. There wasn’t one scheduled.


So while they toured the refinery and went to lunch, I had two hours to put one together. I wasn’t picked because I was the best engineer. I was picked because I had the macro, which made me the only one with a chance. Even with it, the analysis usually took me half a day.


I made it to the meeting on time, the pages still warm from the printer. Page after page, my defense held. Then we reached the last page, where two paragraphs still ended in a bright red XXX. I had to confess. The analysis was done, I just needed five more minutes to write it up. Nobody minded the missing polish. They were stunned it existed at all.


My teammates had known about the macro for a while. They thought it was cool, but nobody had asked for a copy. After that meeting, the first one asked me to set it up on their spreadsheet. That had become the goal, the macro running on every engineer’s report.


I never got there. The planners from that meeting went back to the front office talking about the macro, and the front office had a problem. The software that reconciled yield accounting for the whole refinery was broken. Two years of attempts to fix it had failed, and millions of dollars had gone into them. Fixing it took someone who knew both the process and the software, and I was suddenly the process engineer who understood software. Soon after, I was offered a job in the front office to fix it.


I’d built the macro to save myself a week four times a year. Instead, it handed me a much bigger problem.


### Worth the lift


My professor’s version of lazy stopped at building the system. The first thing I added was picking what to build. Building is work too, and a lazy engineer is just as stingy with it. If you’re going to lift a finger, it should be for the biggest payoff.


That rules out a lot. A bespoke tool for a task you’ll do twice costs more than doing it by hand. So does the universal tool, the one that handles every case anyone can think of. It’s the most work there is, and most of it goes to cases better solved manually.


The lazy move is to find the one approach that covers most of the work, and start there. Small variations pick up much of the rest. What’s left waits until it’s worth the lift, and usually it isn’t.


My macro followed that pattern. Every engineer’s report had the same structure, so one macro could work for all of them, not just me. Trend direction changed from graph to graph, but a small variation handled it. The why was different every time. It took judgment, so it stayed an XXX.


That judgment is where the hard problems live. An AI agent is great at anything that matches a pattern it’s seen before. An answer tangled up in equipment, crude, people, and economics is still yours. Lazy engineers are actually busy. They’re just busy with the hard part.


### Borrow the answer


There’s one more piece my professor left out. The least work of all is solving nothing, because someone in another field already solved it.


After the Exxon Valdez spilled millions of gallons of crude off the coast of Alaska, the cleanup hit a problem nobody in the oil industry could solve. In cold water, the recovered oil and water froze into a slush that couldn’t be pumped out of the barges. Nearly two decades later, still unsolved, it went up on InnoCentive, a site that offers prize money for problems experts couldn’t crack. The winner was John Davis, a chemist who had once spent a summer pouring concrete. He proposed the vibrating rod that keeps fresh concrete flowing, and worried it was too obvious. Nobody in the oil industry had thought of it.


That wasn’t luck. A Harvard Business School study of InnoCentive found that the farther a solver’s expertise was from the problem’s field, the more likely they were to win. My macro was a small version of the same move, nothing new to software but new to a room full of chemical engineers building reports by hand. This series runs it in reverse. A lot of the answers software needs right now are already sitting in a refinery.


### Lazy on purpose


My professor was right. It just took me years to see everything lazy covers. Being lazy isn’t doing less work. It’s refusing to do work a system could do, picking the work with the biggest payoff, and using the answer someone else already found. Then you spend everything you saved on the why. My macro never wrote a word of it. It just bought me the time to.
